note: Passage-centred pack, C1-C2, British English: a spoken mini-talk on post 03's main answer (the stream as a running sum, reads as dot products, the last library entry, probe versus push, and the limits). Levels are AI4Read estimates in the style of the English Vocabulary Profile and English Grammar Profile. Ten headwords are reused from pack 1 or earlier packs where they fit naturally.

passage.text: On our reading, every attention and MLP part adds its write to one shared list, so a language model's hidden state is a running sum. In our toy that is true by construction, and a notebook on GPT-2 small bears it out, up to rounding. Names can mislead: the library's last entry, having been through the final norm, is a case in point, and is not to be taken at face value. To a first approximation, norm aside, a read is a dot product with that sum, so it splits into one share per writer, and a writer at right angles goes unheard. A linear probe is such a read, and a high score shows only that information is present. To say the model therefore uses it would be tantamount to confusing seeing with doing. A steering push shifts every score in lockstep. What a score means, or whether a push changes behaviour, the algebra does not say. Whether concepts are directions in a trained language model's stream hinges on tests that our three sources do not give, so we are on firm ground with the arithmetic, not the interpretation.

gist.question: Why is a model's hidden state described as a running sum?
gist.answer: Because every attention and MLP part adds its write to one shared list, so the state at any point is the sum of the writes made so far.

gist.question: What does a high probe score show, and what does it not show?
gist.answer: It shows only that the information is present; it does not show that the model uses it.

retell.instruction: In 2-3 sentences, explain to a colleague what a hidden state is, what a probe score does and does not show, and what the open question about concepts depends on.
retell.modelAnswer: On our reading, a hidden state is a running sum: every attention and MLP part adds its write, which is true by construction in our toy and holds up to rounding in GPT-2 small, apart from the last library entry. A probe score shows only that information is present, and to say the model uses it would be tantamount to confusing seeing with doing. Whether concepts are directions in a trained language model's stream hinges on tests that our three sources do not give.

items.definition: because of the way something was built or chosen, not because of a discovery
items.sentence: In a simulated network the two communities are denser inside than between by construction, because we wrote the generating rule that way.

items.definition: to show that something said or believed is true
items.sentence: If the replication bears out the original finding, we can report the effect with more confidence.

items.definition: to exist or be said without being noticed, taken into account or dealt with
items.sentence: If we only report the majority label, the minority view among the coders goes unheard.

items.definition: a good example of what has just been said
items.sentence: Proxies can mislead, and follower counts are a case in point.

items.headword: to take something at face value
items.definition: to accept something as it appears, without asking whether it is more complicated
items.sentence: Self-reported media use should not be taken at face value in a survey like this.

items.definition: as a rough first description that ignores smaller details
items.sentence: To a first approximation, we can treat each user as an independent observation, then relax that assumption later.

items.definition: moving or changing together, at exactly the same time and in the same way
items.sentence: If the two series move in lockstep, a single underlying factor may explain both.

items.definition: to have the same effect or meaning as something else, usually something stronger or worse
items.sentence: Treating a correlation as a mechanism would be tantamount to reporting an experiment we never ran.

items.definition: to depend completely on one particular thing
items.sentence: The whole argument hinges on whether the sample resembles the population.

items.definition: in a safe position, with good evidence to support what you say
items.sentence: With the descriptive statistics we are on firm ground; with the causal story, much less so.

items.definition: Put a 'what' clause first, as the object of a verb that comes later, to make it the topic: 'What a score means, the algebra does not say.' The rest keeps normal subject-verb order, and no pronoun is added. It sets what is settled against what is not.
items.anchor: What a score means, or whether a push changes behaviour, the algebra does not say
items.sentence: What a rise in retweets means, the counts alone do not say.
items.target: What a rise in retweets means

items.definition: A 'whether' clause can be the subject of a sentence and takes a singular verb: 'Whether it works hinges on ...'. Use 'whether', not 'if', here, and keep normal word order inside the clause.
items.anchor: Whether concepts are directions in a trained language model's stream
items.sentence: Whether the effect survives a change of sample is a question for the replication.
items.target: Whether the effect survives a change of sample

items.definition: 'Having + past participle' (or 'having been + past participle' in the passive) shows that something was finished, or is the case, before the main clause. The subject of the main clause must be the one the participle clause is about.
items.anchor: having been through the final norm
items.sentence: Having coded every post twice, the team compared the two sets of labels.

items.definition: A noun followed by 'aside' (or 'apart') opens a sentence as a short phrase meaning 'if we set that to one side': 'Norm aside, a read is a dot product'. It is formal, takes no verb, and the noun names the thing being set aside.
items.sentence: Sampling error aside, the two surveys tell much the same story.

items.wrong: To say the model therefore uses it would be tantamount to confuse seeing with doing.
items.definition: Here 'to' is a preposition, not part of an infinitive, so a verb after it takes -ing: tantamount to confusing, not tantamount to confuse. The same holds for amount to, committed to, object to and in addition to.

items.wrong: If concepts are directions in a trained language model's stream hinges on tests that our three sources do not give, so we are on firm ground with the arithmetic, not the interpretation.
items.definition: A clause that is the subject of a sentence begins with 'whether', not 'if': 'Whether it works hinges on ...'. 'If' opens a condition ('if it works, ...'), never a subject clause.

items.wrong: Whether concepts are directions in a trained language model's stream hinges on tests that our three sources do not give, so we are on a firm ground with the arithmetic, not the interpretation.
items.definition: In the idiom 'on firm ground' (also 'on solid ground') there is no article: 'on firm ground', not 'on a firm ground'. Adding 'a' is a common slip.
